def: DNA is a double helix molecule made of two polynucleotide strands, and it is tightly packaged with histone proteins to fit inside the cell nucleus as chromatin.
points: Each strand is a chain of nucleotides; each nucleotide has a sugar (deoxyribose), a phosphate group, and a nitrogenous base.
Bases are A, T, G, C; A pairs with T, and G pairs with C by hydrogen bonds (complementary base pairing).
The two strands run antiparallel and twist into a right-handed double helix (Watson-Crick model).
DNA wraps around a core of 8 histone proteins to form a nucleosome, like beads on a string.
Nucleosomes further coil and condense to form chromatin fibre, and then chromosomes during cell division.
This packaging lets a very long DNA molecule fit compactly inside the small nucleus.
formula: A pairs with T (2 H-bonds); G pairs with C (3 H-bonds)

diagram.draw: Draw two antiparallel strands twisted as a double helix. Mark sugar-phosphate backbone on the outside and base pairs (A-T, G-C) connected by dashed hydrogen bonds on the inside. Separately draw a nucleosome: a disc-shaped histone core with DNA wrapped around it, labelled 'histone octamer' and 'linker DNA'.

example: A nucleosome contains about 200 base pairs of DNA wrapped around 8 histone molecules, repeated thousands of times to form chromatin.
tip: Always mention base-pairing rule (A-T, G-C) with number of hydrogen bonds — a very common 1-mark question.

def: Semiconservative replication is the process by which DNA makes an exact copy of itself, where each new DNA molecule has one old (parental) strand and one newly synthesized strand.
points: The double helix unwinds and the two strands separate, each acting as a template.
DNA polymerase adds complementary nucleotides to each template strand, following base-pairing rules.
This produces two daughter DNA molecules, each with one parental strand and one new strand.
Meselson and Stahl proved this using E. coli grown first in heavy nitrogen (15N) medium, then shifted to normal (14N) medium.
After one generation, DNA showed hybrid (intermediate) density; after two generations, both hybrid and light density DNA appeared.
This matched the semiconservative model and ruled out conservative or dispersive replication models.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Parent DNA (both strands old)"] --> B["Strands separate"]
  B --> C["New strand made on each old strand"]
  C --> D["2 daughter DNA: 1 old + 1 new strand each"]

example: After the first generation in Meselson-Stahl's experiment, all DNA molecules were hybrid density, confirming that each new DNA kept one heavy parental strand.
tip: Name Meselson and Stahl and describe heavy/light nitrogen clearly — the experimental proof is worth separate marks from the concept.

def: Transcription is the synthesis of mRNA from a DNA template, and the genetic code is the set of rules (codons) by which mRNA sequences specify amino acids.
points: RNA polymerase binds to the promoter region of a gene and unwinds the DNA locally.
It synthesizes mRNA complementary to the template strand, in the 5' to 3' direction, using ribonucleotides (with uracil instead of thymine).
Transcription has three stages: initiation, elongation, and termination (at a terminator sequence).
The genetic code is read in triplets called codons; each codon of 3 bases specifies one amino acid.
The code is degenerate (more than one codon can code for the same amino acid) and nearly universal across organisms.
AUG is the start codon (codes for methionine); UAA, UAG, UGA are stop codons.
formula: 64 possible codons; 61 code for amino acids, 3 are stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA)

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["RNA polymerase binds promoter"] --> B["DNA unwinds"]
  B --> C["mRNA synthesized (5' to 3')"]
  C --> D["Termination at stop sequence"]

example: The codon AUG always signals the start of translation and codes for methionine, which is usually the first amino acid of a new polypeptide.
tip: Remember the code is degenerate but unambiguous (one codon never codes for two different amino acids) — this exact wording is often asked.

def: Translation is the process by which ribosomes read mRNA codons and assemble a specific sequence of amino acids to build a polypeptide chain.
points: mRNA attaches to a ribosome, which reads codons starting from the start codon AUG.
tRNA molecules, each carrying a specific amino acid, bring their anticodon to pair with the mRNA codon.
The ribosome forms a peptide bond between consecutive amino acids, growing the polypeptide chain.
The ribosome moves along the mRNA one codon at a time (this movement is called translocation).
Translation stops when the ribosome reaches a stop codon, releasing the finished polypeptide.
The polypeptide then folds and may be modified to become a functional protein.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["mRNA + ribosome"] --> B["tRNA brings amino acid matching codon"]
  B --> C["Peptide bond forms"]
  C --> D["Ribosome moves to next codon"]
  D --> E["Stop codon reached: polypeptide released"]

example: If an mRNA reads AUG-GGA-UUU-UAA, translation produces a chain of 3 amino acids (Met-Gly-Phe) and stops at the UAA stop codon.
tip: Clearly mention the role of tRNA's anticodon matching the mRNA codon — this base-pairing step is the key examiner focus.

def: The lac operon is a group of genes in E. coli (lacZ, lacY, lacA) controlled together by one promoter and operator, switched on only when lactose is available, as a model of gene regulation.
points: The operon has structural genes lacZ, lacY, lacA, controlled by a promoter and operator, and regulated by a separate regulatory gene lacI.
lacI produces a repressor protein that normally binds to the operator, blocking RNA polymerase.
Without lactose: repressor binds operator, transcription is blocked — the operon is 'off'.
With lactose present: allolactose (a lactose derivative) binds to the repressor, changing its shape so it cannot bind the operator.
RNA polymerase can now transcribe the structural genes, producing enzymes needed to digest lactose — the operon is 'on'.
This is an example of negative inducible gene regulation, since a repressor normally keeps genes off until induced.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["No lactose"] --> B["Repressor binds operator"]
  B --> C["Operon OFF"]
  D["Lactose present"] --> E["Allolactose binds repressor"]
  E --> F["Repressor leaves operator"]
  F --> G["Operon ON: enzymes made"]

example: When E. coli is grown in a medium with lactose as the only sugar, lac operon genes switch on within minutes to produce beta-galactosidase for digesting lactose.
tip: Draw both the 'off' state (repressor on operator) and 'on' state (repressor removed) — two separate diagrams fetch separate marks.

def: The Human Genome Project aimed to sequence the entire human genome, and DNA fingerprinting is a technique that uses unique DNA sequence variations (VNTRs) to identify individuals.
points: The Human Genome Project (HGP) was an international effort completed in the early 2000s to determine the sequence of all base pairs in human DNA.
It identified around 20,000-25,000 genes in the human genome and mapped their locations on chromosomes.
HGP findings help in understanding genetic diseases, designing targeted drugs, and advancing personalized medicine.
DNA fingerprinting relies on Variable Number of Tandem Repeats (VNTRs), repetitive DNA sequences that differ in number between individuals.
Steps include isolating DNA, cutting with restriction enzymes, separating fragments by gel electrophoresis, and comparing banding patterns.
Since VNTR patterns are unique to each individual (except identical twins), this technique is used in forensic investigation and paternity testing.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["DNA sample"] --> B["Cut with restriction enzymes"]
  B --> C["Gel electrophoresis"]
  C --> D["Unique VNTR band pattern"]
  D --> E["Match or identify individual"]

example: DNA fingerprinting was used to identify crime suspects and in paternity disputes by comparing VNTR band patterns of the suspect/father with evidence/child samples.
tip: Mention VNTR by name as the basis of DNA fingerprinting — simply saying 'DNA pattern' without this term loses marks.
